messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol had crossed the border from Honduras years before, but the worst night in her life still felt as if it were happening in fragments she could not put away. During the flight north, the van in which she was being transported stopped for a checkpoint, and men in uniforms leaned in close, barking orders over the smell of alcohol on their breath. One of them grabbed her arm as he spoke, and the sharp, sour odor became fused in her mind with the sound of commands, the hard flash of authority, and the knowledge that there was nowhere to go. In the years since, those same cues had kept returning with the force of a warning: a whiff of alcohol in a hallway, a supervisor’s clipped instruction, a correctional officer’s uniform in the prison where she worked as a guard. Each one made her body react before she could think, with a rush of danger that felt immediate and real, and she had come to believe the world was dangerous and people were not what they seemed. At times she looked at herself and could not recognize the woman who had become so watchful and so easily frightened.

Marisol’s life had narrowed around keeping herself from being caught off guard. She avoided being around people in authority or uniform whenever she could, and at work she chose her seat in the break room, the meeting room, even the cafeteria, based on where she would have the most protection at her back and the clearest view of the door. After shifts she turned on loud music or the television just to keep her mind from settling on what had happened. When she found herself dwelling on how the event could have been prevented, she would replay the border crossing over and over, imagining different choices, different routes, different moments where she might have escaped. Those efforts gave her brief relief, but they also kept the event close and made the smell of alcohol, the sound of orders, and the sight of a uniform even more potent, because they returned her attention again and again to what she feared most. The more she tried to keep away from those reminders, the more she felt her world shrinking and her confidence in other people eroding.

Sometimes the memory broke through with startling clarity. She could hear the men’s voices in her head exactly as they had sounded that night, and the scene would come back in such vivid detail that she had to stop whatever she was doing and breathe until the wave of emotion passed. When that happened, she reacted as if danger were right in front of her: a sudden movement nearby in the prison corridor could make her flinch hard enough to embarrass herself, and she would scan every room for exits, certain that something bad was about to happen. The memory and the threat feeling fed each other until she was left with the conviction that she was still in the same kind of danger. After those episodes she became even more convinced that the world could turn hostile without warning, and that she no longer knew herself well enough to trust her own judgment. She would then throw herself back into distraction, turn the TV louder, avoid the officers in uniform at work, and keep choosing the safest seat she could find, but the relief never lasted long. Those habits also gave her fewer opportunities to see that most moments were ordinary, so her fear stayed alive, and the very things she did to steady herself became reminders that she was always bracing for impact.

Recently, the cycle has tightened at the prison. A supervisor’s order delivered across the corridor, the smell of alcohol on an inmate’s breath, or a uniformed sergeant stepping too quickly into her line of sight can set off the same surge of alarm and bring the memory rushing back. Marisol has started calling in sick more often and feels ashamed that she cannot explain to her husband why she is so jumpy and distant. What finally brought her to treatment was realizing that she was living as if every day might collapse into that night again, and that she was exhausted by the effort of staying on guard. She is hoping to feel like herself again, but what she fears most is that the fear will keep spreading until there is nowhere in her life left that feels safe.

violation_explanations: The vignette describes triggers leading to avoidance and distraction, but it does not clearly state the triggers themselves drive those maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows cues provoking alarm, but it does not explicitly state the triggers cause the perceived threat in the required causal way.
The vignette includes negative beliefs, but it does not clearly state the triggers produce those appraisals.
The vignette says negative appraisals are followed by memory replay, but it does not explicitly show the appraisals leading to the intrusive memory.
The vignette does not clearly state that negative appraisals lead Marisol to seek out or notice triggers.
The vignette links memory and negative beliefs, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes the negative appraisals in the required causal way.
The vignette shows threat feelings accompanying memory, but it does not explicitly state the threat feeling drives the memory to intrude.
The vignette does not clearly state that perceived threat leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly state that perceived threat leads to triggering cues or their salience.
The vignette describes maladaptive coping and then memory becoming more accessible, but it does not clearly state the strategies cause the memory intrusions.
The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies generate or worsen negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies lead to triggers or greater trigger exposure/activation.
